description: AstroSUST is a multidisciplinary team from Shahjalal University of Science and Technology (SUST), Bangladesh. We are building TerraTwin, a data-driven platform that uses open Earth, Moon, and Mars datasets to identify and characterize terrestrial analog sites for future lunar and Martian exploration. Our team combines software engineering, AI, GIS, data analysis, and scientific research.
summary: TerraTwin is an interactive 3D tool that finds and characterises Earth terrain analogs for Mars landing and exploration sites from NASA data. Pick any point on Mars: it reads the site's measured terrain from NASA's MOLA altimeter, screens all 249,165 land cells of Earth, then refines the best 50 km windows with Observation-Operator Matching (OOM). The key idea: the MOLA grid is not a direct measurement. Only about one 463 m cell in three holds a laser return; the rest are interpolated. So every Earth candidate is first passed through that Mars site's own MOLA sampling-and-interpolation chain, and Earth and Mars are compared as MOLA would observe both. On a benchmark of 213 synthetic terrain twins this raised exact-twin recovery from 18% to 95%. A leader is named only if it survives four window orientations; otherwise a tie or "no convincing analog" is reported, and an ESA WorldCover gate removes vegetated ground for field-test missions. Verified result: searching the whole Earth for Jezero crater returns a tie of two windows in north-west China (Kunlun-Altun belt, 37.06 N 86.21 E, S 0.781; Qaidam Basin, 37.29 N 97.51 E, S 0.693), each above the classic Atacama analog (S 0.614). Every result states what matches, where the analogy breaks (geology, gravity, atmosphere, radiation), what it can be used for, and exports a dossier with provenance. The method is benchmarked on synthetic twins only and is not yet field-validated.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

TerraTwin answers one question for any site on Mars: where on Earth does the ground look like this to the instrument that mapped Mars, and how far can that analogy be trusted?

1. Select a Mars target. A 3D Mars globe (NASA Mars Trek imagery) carries NASA's 39 candidate human-landing Exploration Zones; any other coordinate can be picked. The inspector shows measured terrain from the USGS MOLA 463 m mosaic (mean slope, 90th-percentile slope, relief, roughness at 0.93, 2.3 and 9.3 km baselines, Hurst exponent), the fraction of MOLA cells actually observed (about 31%), and six NASA context layers: TES thermal inertia, TES rock abundance, USGS SIM 3292 geologic unit, KRC surface temperature, SWIM subsurface-ice consistency and solar energy. Context layers characterise the site and never enter the score.

2. Screen Earth (tier 1). All 249,165 land cells of 25 km (GMTED2010) are scored against the target with the same terrain descriptors, computed by one shared function for both planets on local equal-distance grids built with each planet's own radius. The result is a global similarity field on a 3D Earth globe.

3. Refine with Observation-Operator Matching (tier 2). Shortlisted 50 km Earth windows (Copernicus DEM GLO-90, aggregated to the MOLA grid spacing of 463 m) are passed through the Mars site's own observation chain: the measured MOLA shot-count mask from the NASA PDS MEGDR counts product, an interpolator selected from statistics observable on Mars itself, and the mosaic's measured half-pixel registration. Only then are eight terrain descriptors compared with a transparent log-ratio kernel. No machine learning, no fitted weights.

4. Decide honestly. A single leader is named only if it survives all four orientations of the Earth window relative to MOLA's north-south tracks; otherwise the tool reports a tied set, or "no convincing analog". For field-test missions an ESA WorldCover land-cover gate removes vegetated or water-covered windows before ranking. No score is ever shown without its coverage.

5. Explain and export. Compare mode shows both 50 km windows side by side at one ground scale, every descriptor ratio against its tolerance band, 3D relief of both windows at equal exaggeration, and a Relevance tab listing what was evaluated, what was not, and the planetary differences Earth cannot reproduce (gravity, pressure, atmosphere, radiation). A Report exports a 12-section dossier (JSON, CSV, print) with provenance, verbatim limitations and references. An Evidence page shows the full benchmark, falsification matrix and controls.

WHY IT MATTERS (THE CREATIVE STEP)

The MOLA grid is not a direct measurement: at the 39 Exploration Zones only 31% of 463 m cells contain a laser return; the rest are interpolated. Comparing that grid with densely measured Earth elevation compares a smoothed surface with an unsmoothed one. Passed through the MOLA chain, Earth roughness at 0.93 km drops to 0.69x and the Hurst exponent rises by 0.12, so about half of the apparent Mars-Earth roughness-scaling gap is the data, not the planets. TerraTwin adapts the forward-operator principle of satellite simulators and data assimilation to analog search: Earth and Mars are compared as MOLA would observe both. We did not find this applied to Mars-Earth analog search in our literature search; no priority is claimed.

VERIFIED RESULTS (reproducible in the live app)

- Jezero crater, landing-site profile, live global discovery (40 Copernicus windows refined from the 249,165-cell screen in 41 s): a tie between 37.06 N 86.21 E (Kunlun-Altun mountain belt, south rim of the Tarim Basin, Xinjiang, China; S 0.781) and 37.29 N 97.51 E (north-eastern Qaidam Basin near Delingha, Qinghai, China; S 0.693), both passing the land-cover gate, each above the classic Atacama Yungay analog that leads the fixed 230-window research pool (S 0.614, stable under 4/4 orientations). Other refined windows: southern High Atlas, Morocco (0.774); northern Tibetan Plateau (0.759); Tibesti Mountains, Chad (0.675); west-central Nevada, USA (0.675). Place names are approximate, read from the coordinates by the team; the Qaidam Basin is independently proposed as a Mars analog in the literature; TerraTwin makes no novelty claim.

- Jezero vs the Xinjiang window, as MOLA would see it: mean slope 2.82 vs 2.67 deg; 90th-percentile slope 6.11 vs 5.30 deg; relief 1,763 vs 1,711 m; Hurst 0.678 vs 0.663. Where it breaks: the window is permafrost terrain (probability 1.00, Koppen ET) while Jezero shows no shallow-ice signal; gravity, pressure, atmosphere and radiation differ at any Earth site.

- Method benchmark on 213 synthetic terrain twins (Earth windows degraded through the observation chain of a different zone each): direct comparison recovers the true twin first 18% of the time (MRR 0.30); Observation-Operator Matching 95% (MRR 0.97; delta +0.67, 95% CI 0.62-0.72; 175 targets improved, 0 worse). It beats constant bias correction (0.89) and coverage weighting (0.30); the gain held in 200 of 200 random weight perturbations and all ten roughness deciles. When the tool abstains, the tied set contained the true twin in 35 of 35 cases; when it names a leader, it was correct 98.9% of the time.

- Controls: all six vegetated negative-control regions (Amazon, Congo, Papua New Guinea, West Siberia, Bangladesh, Netherlands) are removed by the gate; 29 of 39 Exploration Zones receive a registration-stable named leader.

IMPACT AND USE

Analog-site selection teams, rover-mobility and landing-hazard algorithm testers, field-campaign planners and students get named, located, measured candidates for any Mars site, beyond the famous analog regions, with the limits attached. Mission profiles (landing site, permanent base, rover mobility, geological exploration, terrain-only) change the descriptor weights.

LIMITATIONS WE STATE UP FRONT

The benefit is shown on synthetic twins only; no ranking has been field-validated or externally reviewed. The MOLA operator is a statistically selected surrogate for an undocumented gridding algorithm; if the true chain were cubic, the correction would hurt (MRR 0.54 vs 0.65), and this adverse test is kept visible. Similarity is terrain geometry only. Rankings depend on the window size and are reported per size; verdict and land-cover thresholds are working assumptions.

TOOLS

Web: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, CesiumJS (two isolated 3D globes), Zustand, TanStack Query, Zod, Motion. API: Python 3.11, FastAPI, Pydantic, NumPy, SciPy, pandas, pyarrow. GIS pipeline: GDAL, pyproj, rasterio. Research code vendored unmodified and SHA-256 checked at every API start. Tests: 82 API tests, 493 web tests, scripted browser journey against production. Hosting: Vercel (front end), AWS Lightsail (API with the 2.1 GB MOLA mosaic, MEGDR counts tiles and 1 km grids).
